headline: A thousand unique transform values is the case that punishes deriving a class from a value: the lanes that keep one class and move the value into a variable or an inline style render eight times faster than the lanes that mint a class per instance.

microbench.why: `next-yak-css-9.7` (0.596 ms/1k) compiles the interpolation into one static class plus a `--var` on each element, so its per-instance work is a number written into a style attribute. `bamboo` (0.637) reaches the same place by a different route: its compiler refuses open runtime values inside `css()`, so the only expressible spelling is a static class plus an inline `style`, which is what the lane ships. The losers all derive a name from the value, `panda` (4.87) minting an arbitrary-value class per element, `styled-components` (4.51) emitting a rule per value through stylis, and `goober` (5.98) compiling and injecting one.

autocannon.why: `next-yak-css-9.7` answers 1,290 req/s on 5.24 kB and `bamboo` 1,110 on 7.49 kB. The lanes that generate CSS per value ship it too: `styled-components` sends 13.8 kB of stylesheet and `emotion` 18.3 kB in every response, and land at 206 and 313 req/s. `panda` at 170 does the per-element resolution without even shipping matching rules.

attribution.why: `next-yak-css-9.7` (0.750 ms) and `bamboo` (0.783) are react-dom plus a style attribute, with library slices of 0.257 and 0.000 ms. `styled-components` puts 4.74 of its 5.26 ms into the library, and the profile names the reason: 52.6 ms of stylis in a 142 ms JS window, parsing one new rule per instance. `panda` puts 5.35 of 5.92 ms into component self-time and 142 ms into its own package building class names such as `transform_translateX(1px)` that the extracted sheet has no rule for. `goober` is the extreme at 6.80 ms with 162 ms inside itself.

hydrate.why: Where the sheet is finished, hydration is 49.0-54.8 ms of JS with no style or layout in the span. `goober` needs 1,330 ms: it injects a thousand distinct classes into the document during hydration, which is the single largest number anywhere in the study. `styled-components` (117 ms) and `emotion` (102) pay a smaller version of the same bill, and `panda` (72.3 ms) re-derives its arbitrary-value names on the client.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

inp.why: Changing one element's transform touches one class or one style attribute, so almost every lane lands in a 6.7-9.8 ms cluster that is one measurement wide. High cardinality barely reaches a single interaction, since only one new value has to be handled. `panda` (22.3 ms), `goober` (22.7) and `panda-props` (30.0) are the exceptions, each re-deriving a name for the value that changed.

mount.why: 65.7-72.2 ms for every lane that mounts a finished sheet, `bamboo` (68.3 ms) included. `goober` reaches 1,320 ms, injecting a thousand rules before it can paint. `emotion` (121 ms) and `styled-components` (116) parse the thousand-rule sheet they shipped, and `panda` (90.1) resolves its per-element names.

renderTiming.why: One recalculation and one layout in every lane, so the counts tie; the transform is a compositor-friendly property and none of the spellings forces extra work. The recalculation costs 0.078-0.186 ms across the whole field, which is where the case's cost is not.

payload.why: This is where deriving CSS from data shows up plainly. `next-yak-css-9.7` ships 105 B of stylesheet, because a thousand different transforms are one rule with a variable in it; `emotion` ships 18.3 kB and `styled-components` 13.8 kB of stylesheet, one rule per value. `bamboo` at 7.49 kB and `panda` at 10.4 keep their sheet small and put the value in the markup instead.

nsweep.why: `next-yak-css-9.7` (2.66 ms at n=4,000), `vanilla` (2.68) and `bamboo` (2.73) are linear and flat, since per-instance work is one attribute write. `panda` reaches 22.5 ms and `styled-components` 19.7. `goober` at 164 ms is superlinear, its injection cost growing with the number of rules already in the sheet.

crossCase: This is the naive spelling of the Example `dyn-fair` shown below, where each library uses its own documented answer to a runtime value. next-yak needs no such answer: it compiles the interpolation into a class plus a custom property either way, so `next-yak-css-9.7` costs 0.596 ms/1k here and 0.617 there. Everyone else moves by the width of the case: `goober` 5.98 to 1.06 ms/1k and 1,320 to 86.1 ms of cold mount, `styled-components` 4.51 to 1.35 and 35.3 to 18.9 kB of payload, `panda` 4.87 to 1.15, `cnfast` 1.89 to 0.640. That improvement is a build-time optimization performed by hand, per component, on every dynamic value, forever, and `dyn-translate` is what the same code costs the day nobody performs it. `bamboo` is the third route: its compiler rejects a runtime value inside `css()` outright, so the lane's two files are the same code and its two figures are the same figure (0.637 and 0.633 ms/1k). The Example `dyn-inline` shown below strips the question back further and prices next-yak's variable indirection against a plain inline style.
